title: Places and journeys
job: A trip told in full, with directions inside it
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: al- + N + alladhī + V + fīhi / fīhā
khudh + al- + N + alladhī + V + ilā + <place>

rules.text: THE RELATIVE PRONOUN AGREES AND IS OBLIGATORY: alladhī for a masculine antecedent, allatī for a feminine, alladhīna for a human plural. It is chosen by the noun in FRONT of it, and Arabic cannot drop it the way English drops that.
English drops the relative whenever it can — the bus going to the market, the hotel we stayed in. After a definite Arabic noun it is required, and its absence leaves the clause hanging on nothing.
THE INDEFINITE ANTECEDENT TAKES NO PRONOUN AT ALL: raʾaytu rajul yaqif amāma al-bāb, I saw a man standing at the door. The clause simply follows, and inserting alladhī here is an error.

THE RESUMPTIVE PRONOUN. When the noun is the object of a preposition inside the clause, Arabic keeps a pronoun for it: al-funduq alladhī nazalnā fīhi — the hotel that we stayed in IT. English forbids that pronoun; Arabic requires it.

WHERE THE L1 HELPS: word order inside the clause is ordinary Arabic order and nothing moves. Unlike English there is no fronting to learn — the verb stays where a verb goes and the pronoun stays where the preposition put it.
The trip itself is told in the plain past: sāfartu ilā, then L2-M4's bi- for the means. The directions are L2-M4's too, and what this module adds is only the clause that hangs one off a noun.

sentences.display: khudh al-ḥāfila allatī tadhhab ilā as-sūq
sentences.script: خذ الحافلة التي تذهب إلى السوق
sentences.cue: Take the bus that goes to the market
sentences.literal: Take the-bus which-fem she-goes to the-market

words.note: The relative pronoun for a feminine antecedent. Arabic cannot drop it the way English drops that, and it agrees with the noun in front, not with anything in the clause.

sentences.trap: English drops the relative freely — take the bus going to the market. Arabic cannot: with a DEFINITE noun in front, allatī or alladhī is obligatory and its absence is heard as an unfinished sentence.
sentences.sound: al-la-TĪ: the doubled l is held, so the word has a small hitch in the middle before the long ī.

variations.display: khudhī al-ḥāfila allatī tadhhab ilā as-sūq
variations.script: خذي الحافلة التي تذهب إلى السوق
variations.cue: Take the bus that goes to the market (to a woman)
variations.changed: who is being told — L2-M4's feminine imperative, with the relative untouched

variations.display: khudh al-ḥāfila allatī tadhhab ilā al-maḥaṭṭa
variations.script: خذ الحافلة التي تذهب إلى المحطة
variations.cue: Take the bus that goes to the station
variations.changed: where the bus goes

mistake.why: The relative dropped, English-style. After a definite noun the clause has nothing to hang on, and the sentence reads as two commands stuck together.

sentences.usage: Turning a direction into part of the thing you are pointing at.
sentences.mnemonic: A definite noun keeps its allatī; English is the language that throws it away.

sentences.display: hādhā huwa ash-shāriʿ alladhī yadhhab ilā al-maḥaṭṭa
sentences.script: هذا هو الشارع الذي يذهب إلى المحطة
sentences.cue: This is the street that goes to the station
sentences.literal: This he the-street which-masc he-goes to the-station

words.note: The masculine relative. Which one you use is decided by the noun in FRONT of it, never by the verb behind it.
The street. L2-M4 gave the directions but never this word; the article assimilates to the sh.
The road, longer and less urban than a shāriʿ. It is also the way to somewhere, in the sense a direction takes.

sentences.trap: English uses one word — that — for every gender and number. Arabic makes you look back at the noun before you can start the clause, which is the opposite direction of travel.
sentences.sound: al-la-DHĪ: the dh is the voiced th of English this, and again the l in front of it is doubled and held.

variations.display: hādhā huwa aṭ-ṭarīq alladhī yadhhab ilā al-maṭār
variations.script: هذا هو الطريق الذي يذهب إلى المطار
variations.cue: This is the road that goes to the airport
variations.changed: the noun, and with it where the road ends

variations.display: hādhihi hiya al-ḥāfila allatī tadhhab ilā as-sūq
variations.script: هذه هي الحافلة التي تذهب إلى السوق
variations.cue: This is the bus that goes to the market
variations.changed: a feminine antecedent, so hādhihi, hiya and allatī all move together

mistake.display: hādhā huwa ash-shāriʿ allatī yadhhab ilā al-maḥaṭṭa
mistake.script: هذا هو الشارع التي يذهب إلى المحطة
mistake.why: A feminine relative on a masculine noun. The agreement is with ash-shāriʿ in front; the verb behind it is already masculine and cannot rescue the pronoun.

sentences.usage: Pointing something out and saying what it is for in one sentence.
sentences.mnemonic: Look backwards to pick the pronoun, forwards to use it.

sentences.display: raʾaytu an-nās alladhīna yaʿmalūn fī al-maṭār
sentences.script: رأيت الناس الذين يعملون في المطار
sentences.cue: I saw the people who work at the airport
sentences.literal: I-saw the-people who-pl they-work in the-airport

words.note: People, as a collective. It is grammatically plural and human, which is what decides the relative pronoun in front of the clause.
The relative for a HUMAN plural. A non-human plural takes allatī instead, as though it were one feminine thing.
The they-cell of L2-M8's yaʿmal. No mood ending is written, so the plural ends on the bare -ūn.

sentences.trap: English who and that are indifferent to number. Arabic has a third relative for human plurals only, and choosing it means deciding whether the noun counts as people or as things.
sentences.sound: al-la-DHĪ-na: the same word as alladhī with a -na tail; the stress stays on the long ī.

variations.display: raʾaytu an-nās alladhīna yaʿmalūn fī al-maḥaṭṭa
variations.script: رأيت الناس الذين يعملون في المحطة
variations.cue: I saw the people who work at the station
variations.changed: where they work

variations.display: sāfartu maʿa an-nās alladhīna yaʿmalūn fī al-maṭār
variations.script: سافرت مع الناس الذين يعملون في المطار
variations.cue: I travelled with the people who work at the airport
variations.changed: the main clause, from seeing to travelling

mistake.display: raʾaytu an-nās allatī yaʿmalūn fī al-maṭār
mistake.script: رأيت الناس التي يعملون في المطار
mistake.why: allatī on a human plural. allatī is for a feminine singular or a non-human plural; people take alladhīna.

sentences.usage: Describing a group by what they do.
sentences.mnemonic: alladhīna is for people you could count.

sentences.cue: I saw a man standing in front of the door

words.note: A man. Thirty modules in, the word is new: the course has had ṣadīq, mudīr and muwaẓẓaf but never the plain noun.
He stands or is standing. Arabic has no separate continuous, so the plain present covers both.
In front of. It takes a noun directly, with no preposition between them.

sentences.trap: English needs a man WHO is standing, or a participle. Arabic forbids the relative here: after an INDEFINITE noun the clause simply follows, and inserting alladhī is the error.
sentences.sound: YA-qif: the q is deep against the soft palate, and the word ends on a bare f with no vowel behind it.

variations.display: raʾaytu imraʾa taqif amāma al-bāb
variations.script: رأيت امرأة تقف أمام الباب
variations.cue: I saw a woman standing in front of the door
variations.changed: who was standing, so the verb takes the t- prefix

variations.display: raʾaytu ar-rajul alladhī yaqif amāma al-bāb
variations.script: رأيت الرجل الذي يقف أمام الباب
variations.cue: I saw the man who is standing in front of the door
variations.changed: the noun made DEFINITE — which is exactly what forces alladhī back in

mistake.display: raʾaytu rajul alladhī yaqif amāma al-bāb
mistake.script: رأيت رجل الذي يقف أمام الباب
mistake.why: A relative pronoun after an indefinite noun. English inserts one and Arabic forbids one; the pair with the variation above is the whole rule.

sentences.usage: Reporting what you saw on the way.
sentences.mnemonic: Definite takes the pronoun, indefinite takes nothing.

sentences.display: al-funduq alladhī nazalnā fīhi kāna jamīl
sentences.script: الفندق الذي نزلنا فيه كان جميل
sentences.cue: The hotel that we stayed in was beautiful
sentences.literal: The-hotel which-masc we-stayed in-it was beautiful

words.note: The hotel. It is masculine, which is what picks alladhī in front of the clause.
We stayed — the verb for putting up somewhere, not for remaining. It reaches its place through fī.
L1-M7's fī with a pronoun stuck on. Inside a relative clause it is the RESUMPTIVE pronoun, and it is obligatory.

sentences.trap: English forbids the pronoun absolutely — the hotel that we stayed in IT is not English. Arabic requires it, and nothing in the L1 prepares a learner to leave it standing.
sentences.sound: FĪ-hi: two light syllables; the h is the ordinary light one, not the throat ḥ.

variations.display: al-funduq alladhī nazaltu fīhi kāna jamīl
variations.script: الفندق الذي نزلت فيه كان جميل
variations.cue: The hotel that I stayed in was beautiful
variations.changed: who stayed — the resumptive pronoun does not move

variations.display: al-funduq alladhī nazalnā fīhi kāna qarīb min al-maṭār
variations.script: الفندق الذي نزلنا فيه كان قريب من المطار
variations.cue: The hotel that we stayed in was near the airport
variations.changed: what is said about the hotel once the clause closes

mistake.why: The resumptive pronoun dropped, English-style. nazalnā needs a place, and inside the clause that place can only be fīhi — without it the clause is about nothing.

sentences.usage: Telling someone about a stay after it is over.
sentences.mnemonic: English throws the pronoun out; Arabic keeps it in.

sentences.display: al-qarya allatī nazalnā fīhā kānat ṣaghīra
sentences.script: القرية التي نزلنا فيها كانت صغيرة
sentences.cue: The village that we stayed in was small
sentences.literal: The-village which-fem we-stayed in-it-fem was small

words.note: A village, smaller than L3-M10's madīna. It is feminine, so everything downstream of it is too.
The feminine resumptive. Its ending agrees with the antecedent, exactly as allatī does, so the two always match.

sentences.trap: English has one pronoun, it, and forbids it here anyway. Arabic has a masculine and a feminine one and requires whichever the antecedent chose, two words back.
sentences.sound: fī-HĀ: the long ā at the end takes the stress, which is the only audible difference from fīhi.

variations.display: al-madīna allatī nazalnā fīhā kānat kabīra
variations.script: المدينة التي نزلنا فيها كانت كبيرة
variations.cue: The city that we stayed in was big
variations.changed: the antecedent — still feminine, so nothing else moves

variations.display: al-qarya allatī nazalnā fīhā kānat jamīla
variations.script: القرية التي نزلنا فيها كانت جميلة
variations.cue: The village that we stayed in was beautiful
variations.changed: what is said about it

mistake.display: al-qarya allatī nazalnā fīhi kānat ṣaghīra
mistake.script: القرية التي نزلنا فيه كانت صغيرة
mistake.why: A masculine resumptive under a feminine antecedent. allatī and fīhā are two halves of one agreement and cannot disagree.

sentences.usage: Describing a place you passed through.
sentences.mnemonic: allatī above, fīhā below: they agree or the clause breaks.

sentences.cue: I travelled to the airport by train

words.note: To travel, of a journey between places. It reaches its destination through ilā, never bare.
The airport. It joins L2-M4's maḥaṭṭa, the station, as a place a journey starts or ends.

sentences.trap: English travelled TO and went TO look alike, so the preposition feels optional. With sāfara it is not: the verb cannot take its destination directly.
sentences.sound: sā-FAR-tu: the first ā is long, and the stress sits on the middle syllable.

variations.display: sāfara ṣadīqī ilā al-maṭār bi-al-ḥāfila
variations.script: سافر صديقي إلى المطار بالحافلة
variations.cue: My friend travelled to the airport by bus
variations.changed: who travelled and how — L2-M4's bi- of means, untouched

variations.display: sāfartu ilā al-madīna bi-al-qiṭār
variations.script: سافرت إلى المدينة بالقطار
variations.cue: I travelled to the city by train
variations.changed: where the journey ended

mistake.why: sāfara with a bare destination. The verb needs ilā to reach a place, and without it the airport reads as something the traveller did rather than somewhere they went.

sentences.usage: The opening line of an account of a trip.

sentences.display: kānat ar-riḥla ṭawīla, wa lākin al-manẓar kāna jamīl
sentences.script: كانت الرحلة طويلة، ولكن المنظر كان جميل
sentences.cue: The trip was long, but the view was beautiful
sentences.literal: Was the-trip long, and but the-view was beautiful

words.note: The journey as a whole thing, not the travelling. It is feminine, so kānat and ṭawīla follow it.
What you can see from where you are. It is masculine, which is why the second half of the sentence changes shape.

sentences.trap: English keeps was and long the same whoever they belong to. Arabic bends both to the noun, so one sentence with two subjects has two sets of endings.
sentences.sound: ar-RIḤ-la: the ḥ in the middle is the breathy throat one, and it closes the first syllable.

variations.display: kānat ar-riḥla qaṣīra, wa lākin al-manẓar kāna jamīl
variations.script: كانت الرحلة قصيرة، ولكن المنظر كان جميل
variations.cue: The trip was short, but the view was beautiful
variations.changed: the adjective on the first half

variations.display: kānat ar-riḥla ṭawīla, wa lākin al-funduq kāna jamīl
variations.script: كانت الرحلة طويلة، ولكن الفندق كان جميل
variations.cue: The trip was long, but the hotel was beautiful
variations.changed: what the second half is about

mistake.display: kāna ar-riḥla ṭawīl, wa lākin al-manẓar kānat jamīla
mistake.script: كان الرحلة طويل، ولكن المنظر كانت جميلة
mistake.why: The two agreements swapped. riḥla is feminine and manẓar is masculine, and every word attached to each has to know it.

sentences.usage: The verdict at the end of a journey.
sentences.mnemonic: The noun decides; kāna and the adjective obey.

sentences.display: idhhab mustaqīm ḥattā taṣil ilā al-maḥaṭṭa
sentences.script: اذهب مستقيم حتى تصل إلى المحطة
sentences.cue: Go straight until you reach the station
sentences.literal: Go straight until you-arrive to the-station

words.note: Straight on. It sits behind the verb of going as a description of the going, with no preposition.

sentences.trap: English go straight and go straight ON are interchangeable, so a learner looks for a particle to add. Arabic adds nothing: the adjective stands bare after the command.
sentences.sound: mus-ta-QĪM: the q is the deep one and the long ī carries the stress.

variations.display: idhhab mustaqīm ḥattā taṣil ilā ash-shāriʿ
variations.script: اذهب مستقيم حتى تصل إلى الشارع
variations.cue: Go straight until you reach the street
variations.changed: where the walking ends

variations.display: khudh aṭ-ṭarīq alladhī yadhhab ilā al-maḥaṭṭa
variations.script: خذ الطريق الذي يذهب إلى المحطة
variations.cue: Take the road that goes to the station
variations.changed: the same direction given as a relative clause instead of a command

mistake.display: idhhab mustaqīm ḥattā waṣalta ilā al-maḥaṭṭa
mistake.script: اذهب مستقيم حتى وصلت إلى المحطة
mistake.why: A past verb behind ḥattā for an arrival still ahead. L4-M6 set the rule: a present shape for what has not happened, a past for what was reached.

sentences.mnemonic: The direction is bare; the relative clause is the fancy way.

sentences.display: raʾaytu imraʾa taqif amāma al-funduq alladhī nazalnā fīhi
sentences.script: رأيت امرأة تقف أمام الفندق الذي نزلنا فيه
sentences.cue: I saw a woman standing in front of the hotel that we stayed in
sentences.literal: I-saw woman she-stands in-front-of the-hotel which-masc we-stayed in-it

words.note: A woman. The hamza sits in the middle and is written ʾ; the word is rajul's pair and is new for the same reason.

sentences.trap: English would tie the whole thing together with two thats. Arabic uses none for the indefinite woman and one for the definite hotel, in the same breath — the two laws working against each other.
sentences.sound: im-RA-ʾa: the hamza before the final a is a small catch, not a vowel of its own.

variations.display: raʾaytu imraʾa taqif amāma al-maḥaṭṭa
variations.script: رأيت امرأة تقف أمام المحطة
variations.cue: I saw a woman standing in front of the station
variations.changed: the place, with the second clause dropped

variations.display: raʾaytu al-imraʾa allatī taqif amāma al-funduq
variations.script: رأيت المرأة التي تقف أمام الفندق
variations.cue: I saw the woman who is standing in front of the hotel
variations.changed: the woman made definite, which pulls allatī in and pushes the second clause out

mistake.why: A definite antecedent with no relative. Making the noun definite is exactly what obliges allatī, and the two errors of this module are one decision apart.

sentences.usage: Closing an account of a trip on the thing you remember.
sentences.mnemonic: One sentence, both laws: nothing after a woman, alladhī after the hotel.
